    role: background
    relevance: >
      First study on overoptimization in composite reward models. Shows that
      fixed-weight linear scalarization of component rewards leads to
      degradation past a threshold. Proposes constrained RL with dynamic
      Lagrange multiplier weighting as alternative to fixed ISR weight.
    key_finding: >
      Correlation between component RMs significantly affects overoptimization
      thresholds. Constrained RL with Lagrange multipliers outperforms
      fixed-weight reward composition.

  - id: skalse-reward-hacking
    title: "Defining and Characterizing Reward Hacking"
    authors: "Joar Skalse, Nikolaus H. R. Howe, Dmitrii Krasheninnikov, David Krueger"
    year: 2022
    venue: "arXiv 2209.13085 / NeurIPS 2022"
    category: reward-shaping
    role: background
    relevance: >
      Formal proof that for stochastic policies, two reward functions are
      unhackable only if one is constant. Theoretically explains why any
      non-zero ISR weight can decrease prove_rate -- this is a fundamental
      property of reward composition, not STA-specific.
    key_finding: >
      Any non-constant proxy reward can decrease true reward when optimized.
      Unhackability requires the proxy to be constant, making all non-trivial
      auxiliary rewards theoretically vulnerable to degrading primary performance.

  - id: progrs-outcome-conditioned
    title: "LLM Reasoning with Process Rewards for Outcome-Guided Steps"
    authors: "Mohammad Rezaei, Jens Lehmann, Sahar Vahdati"
    year: 2026
    venue: "arXiv 2604.02341"
    category: reward-shaping
    role: background
    relevance: >
      PRM scores optimized as absolute rewards amplify fluent failure modes.
      Outcome-conditioned centering shifts incorrect trajectories' PRM scores
      to zero mean, preserving ranking info without corrupting gradients.
      Suggests STA should condition ISR on execution outcome.
    key_finding: >
      Naive process rewards induce reward hacking by rewarding locally fluent
      but globally incorrect reasoning. Outcome-conditioned centering resolves
      the conflict with fewer rollouts than outcome-only baselines.

  - id: qwen-prm-lessons
    title: "The Lessons of Developing Process Reward Models in Mathematical Reasoning"
    authors: "Zhenru Zhang et al. (Qwen Team, Alibaba)"
    year: 2025
    venue: "ACL 2025 Findings (arXiv 2501.07301)"
    category: reward-shaping
    role: supporting-evidence
    relevance: >
      MC estimation-synthesized PRM data leads to quality degradation; policy
      model generates "answer-correct but reasoning-flawed" responses, causing
      process reward / outcome misalignment. Directly parallels ISR problem:
      structurally correct but semantically wrong proof traces get high ISR
      but low execution reward.
    key_finding: >
      PRM performance depends critically on data quality; MC estimation
      introduces systematic bias. Answer-correct reasoning-flawed samples
      corrupt process supervision signal.

  # ============================================================
  # Category 3: Mutation testing in software engineering
  # ============================================================

  - id: demillo1978
    title: "Hints on Test Data Selection: Help for the Practicing Programmer"
    authors: "Richard A. DeMillo, Richard J. Lipton, Frederick G. Sayward"
    year: 1978
    venue: "Computer 11(4):34-43"
    category: mutation-testing
    role: background
    relevance: >
      Foundational paper introducing mutation testing. STA's component
      necessity testing directly extends this idea: instead of mutating
      source code to test test suites, STA mutates logical formulas
      to test component necessity for solver success.
    key_finding: >
      Introduced mutation testing and the coupling effect hypothesis:
      tests that detect simple faults also detect complex faults.

  - id: offutt-coupling
    title: "Investigations of the Software Testing Coupling Effect"
    authors: "A. Jefferson Offutt"
    year: 1992
    venue: "ACM TOSEM 1(1):5-20"
    category: mutation-testing
    role: background
    relevance: >
      Empirically validates the coupling effect hypothesis that underpins
      mutation testing. STA's single-component ablation is analogous to
      first-order mutation; the coupling effect suggests this suffices.
    key_finding: >
      Test data killing all first-order mutants killed >99% of second-
      and third-order mutants, validating the coupling effect.

  - id: jia-harman-survey
    title: "An Analysis and Survey of the Development of Mutation Testing"
    authors: "Yue Jia, Mark Harman"
    year: 2011
    venue: "IEEE TSE 37(5):649-678"
    category: mutation-testing
    role: background
    relevance: >
      Comprehensive survey of mutation testing covering three decades of
      development. Provides theoretical and practical foundation for STA's
      adaptation of mutation testing to logical formulas.
    key_finding: >
      Systematic classification of mutation operators, cost reduction
      techniques, and equivalence problem -- all relevant to STA's design
      of clause-level ablation operators.

  - id: just-mutants-real-faults
    title: "Are Mutants a Valid Substitute for Real Faults in Software Testing?"
    authors: "Rene Just, Darioush Jalali, Laura Inozemtseva, et al."
    year: 2014
    venue: "FSE 2014"
    category: mutation-testing
    role: background
    relevance: >
      Validates that mutation testing (structural/intensional analysis of
      program adequacy) correlates with real fault detection. Supports STA's
      premise that structural analysis of formalization components provides
      meaningful signal about formalization quality.
    key_finding: >
      Mutant detection is statistically correlated with real fault detection,
      and mutation score is a better predictor of test effectiveness than
      code coverage.

  - id: llmorpheus
    title: "LLMorpheus: Mutation Testing Using Large Language Models"
    authors: "Frank Tip, Jon Bell, et al."
    year: 2025
    venue: "IEEE TSE 2025"
    category: mutation-testing
    role: background
    relevance: >
      Uses LLMs to generate realistic code mutants beyond traditional
      mutation operators. Shows mutation testing evolving toward
      ML-integrated approaches, validating STA's cross-pollination
      of mutation testing ideas into ML training.
    key_finding: >
      LLM-generated mutants simulate real bugs that rule-based operators
      cannot produce, improving mutation testing realism.

  - id: mutation-guided-meta
    title: "Mutation-Guided LLM-based Test Generation at Meta"
    authors: "Christopher Foster et al."
    year: 2025
    venue: "FSE 2025"
    category: mutation-testing
    role: background
    relevance: >
      Industrial application of mutation-guided LLM test generation at
      Meta. Demonstrates that mutation analysis can guide LLM behavior
      in production -- analogous to how STA uses mutation (ablation) to
      guide GRPO reward signal.
    key_finding: >
      Mutation-guided approach generates tests that kill significantly
      more mutants than unguided LLM test generation at Meta scale.

  - id: mutation-consistency-llm
    title: "Mutation-based Consistency Testing for Evaluating the Code Understanding Capability of LLMs"
    authors: "Various"
    year: 2024
    venue: "arXiv 2401.05940"
    category: mutation-testing
    role: background
    relevance: >
      Uses code mutations to evaluate LLM code understanding consistency.

      mutations to assess model capabilities.
    key_finding: >
      LLMs show significant inconsistency when evaluated on mutated code
      variants, suggesting superficial pattern matching.

  # Category 4: Intensional program analysis
  # ============================================================

    key_finding: >
      Probabilistic mutation framework enables meaningful test adequacy
      assessment for neural networks through structural perturbation.

  # Category 5: Reward hacking / overoptimization
  # ============================================================

  - id: inform-reward-hacking
    title: "InfoRM: Mitigating Reward Hacking in RLHF via Information-Theoretic Reward Modeling"

    year: 2024
    venue: "NeurIPS 2024"

    key_finding: >
      Variational information bottleneck filters irrelevant features from
      reward model; Cluster Separation Index detects reward overoptimization.

  - id: mo-grpo
    title: "MO-GRPO: Mitigating Reward Hacking of Group Relative Policy Optimization on Multi-Objective Problems"
    authors: "CyberAgent AI Lab"
    year: 2025
    venue: "arXiv 2509.22047"

      Standard GRPO normalizes after summing rewards, allowing high-variance
      objectives to dominate. MO-GRPO equalizes scales before aggregation.

    title: "Reward Hacking in the Era of Large Models: Mechanisms, Emergent Misalignment, Challenges"
    authors: "Various"
    year: 2026

    role: background

    year: 2025
    venue: "ICML 2025"

      structural reward approach.
    key_finding: >
      Energy loss in the final layer increases during RL and excessive
      increase characterizes reward hacking; EPPO algorithm penalizes
      this to mitigate hacking.

  - id: spurious-rewards
    title: "Spurious Rewards: Rethinking Training Signals in RLVR"
    authors: "Ruixin Yang et al."
    year: 2025
    venue: "arXiv 2506.10947 / NeurIPS 2025 submission"

    role: direct-evidence
    relevance: >
      Most directly relevant to STA findings. GRPO+random reward on
      Qwen2.5-Math improves 21.4%, nearly matching ground-truth reward's
      29.1%. Matches our plan017 finding: additive random (PR=48%) >
      additive ISR (PR=18%). Structured metrics can be worse than random
      noise due to systematic bias vs pure variance.
    key_finding: >
      Random reward nearly matches ground-truth reward in GRPO training,
      suggesting GRPO's group normalization extracts signal from noise.
      Effect is model-dependent (works on Qwen2.5, not Llama3).

  - id: gao-reward-overoptimization
    title: "Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization"
    authors: "Leo Gao, John Schulman, Jacob Hilton"
    year: 2023
    venue: "ICML 2023 (arXiv 2210.10760)"
    category: reward-hacking
    role: theoretical-foundation
    relevance: >
      Foundational work quantifying Goodhart's effect: proxy reward rises
      but gold reward first rises then falls. ISR is a proxy reward that
      exhibits exactly this pattern — ISR can increase while prove_rate
      decreases, making it suitable for post-hoc diagnosis but harmful
      as training signal.
    key_finding: >
      Gold/proxy reward divergence follows predictable scaling laws.
      Proxy reward optimization past critical point degrades gold reward,
      with the divergence point scaling with model and dataset size.

  - id: karwowski-goodhart-rl
    title: "Goodhart's Law in Reinforcement Learning"
    authors: "Jacek Karwowski, Oliver Hayman, Xingjian Bai, Klaus Kiendlhofer, Charlie Griffin, Joar Skalse"
    year: 2024
    venue: "ICLR 2024 (arXiv 2310.09144)"
    category: reward-hacking
    role: theoretical-foundation
    relevance: >
      Geometric interpretation of Goodhart's Law in MDPs: optimizing
      imperfect proxy past critical point decreases true objective. ISR as
      proxy has partial correlation with execution correctness — exceeding
      critical optimization point pushes policy toward high-ISR but
      low-correctness regions. Explains plan002/plan005 negative results.
    key_finding: >
      Formalizes Goodhart's Law for RL: any non-trivially correlated proxy
      reward creates regions where proxy and true reward diverge, and
      policy optimization inevitably enters these regions.

      drops past capability thresholds. More capable optimization produces

1	# Goodhart's Law in RL — Literature Survey
2	
3	## Category 1: Reward Overoptimization in RLHF
4	
5	### Core Papers
6	
7	- **Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization** (Gao, Schulman & Hilton, 2023, ICML)
8	  - Key finding: Gold reward initially increases then decreases as optimization against proxy RM intensifies — direct empirical Goodhart demonstration. The overoptimization relationship follows different functional forms for RL vs. best-of-n, coefficients scale smoothly with RM parameter count. KL penalties increase achievable proxy reward at a given KL but do not improve the gold-reward frontier.
9	  - Relevance: Foundational paper. Our ISR dose-response (β=0.1 helps, β=0.3 hurts) is a precise instance of their inverted-U curve, but in a neurosymbolic verification setting rather than language preference.
10	  - BibTeX key: `gao2023scaling`
11	
12	- **Defining and Characterizing Reward Hacking** (Skalse, Howe, Krasheninnikov & Krueger, 2022, NeurIPS)
13	  - Key finding: First formal definition of reward hacking. Proves that for stochastic policies, non-trivial unhackable proxy-true reward pairs do not exist (unless one is constant). Establishes reward hacking as a near-universal theoretical concern.
14	  - Relevance: Provides the theoretical impossibility result that frames why our ISR hacking is expected, not anomalous.
15	  - BibTeX key: `skalse2022defining`
16	
17	- **Categorizing Variants of Goodhart's Law** (Manheim & Garrabrant, 2019, arXiv)
18	  - Key finding: Four-part taxonomy: (1) Regressional — extreme proxy values overestimate true goal; (2) Extremal — proxy-goal relationship breaks in OOD regions; (3) Causal — non-causal correlations fail under intervention; (4) Adversarial — optimization creates gaming incentives.
19	  - Relevance: Our high-β ISR collapse is best classified as extremal Goodhart (policy moves to OOD region where ISR↑ but PR↓). Provides vocabulary for discussion section.
20	  - BibTeX key: `manheim2019categorizing`
21	
22	- **The Effects of Reward Misspecification: Mapping and Mitigating Misaligned Models** (Pan, Bhatia & Steinhardt, 2022, ICLR)
23	  - Key finding: Across 9 environments, more capable agents exploit misspecifications more. Observes phase transitions — capability thresholds where true reward sharply drops. Proposes anomaly detection as mitigation.
24	  - Relevance: Their "phase transition" pattern matches our β=0.1→0.3 discontinuity. More capable optimization = worse outcome under misspecification.
25	  - BibTeX key: `pan2022effects`
26	
27	- **Confronting Reward Model Overoptimization with Constrained RLHF** (Moskovitz, Singh, Strouse et al., 2024, ICLR Spotlight)
28	  - Key finding: First study of overoptimization in composite reward models. Correlation between component RMs affects overoptimization onset. Proposes constrained RL to prevent exceeding each component's "threshold of usefulness."
29	  - Relevance: Directly applicable — our setup combines exec reward + ISR reward. Their "threshold of usefulness" concept maps to our optimal β.
30	  - BibTeX key: `moskovitz2024confronting`
31	
32	- **Catastrophic Goodhart: Regularizing RLHF with KL Divergence Does Not Mitigate Heavy-Tailed Reward Misspecification** (Kwa, Thomas & Garriga-Alonso, 2024, NeurIPS)
33	  - Key finding: If reward model error is heavy-tailed, policies can achieve arbitrarily high proxy reward with no true utility gain. KL regularization provably fails under heavy-tailed misspecification.
34	  - Relevance: Raises the question of whether our ISR error distribution is heavy-tailed — if so, explains why KL penalty alone cannot prevent collapse at high β.
35	  - BibTeX key: `kwa2024catastrophic`
36	
37	### Survey & Background
38	
39	- **Concrete Problems in AI Safety** (Amodei, Olah, Steinhardt et al., 2016, arXiv)
40	  - Key finding: Identifies reward hacking as one of five practical AI safety problems. Discusses exploitation through environmental complexity and hard-to-formalize concepts.
41	  - Relevance: Classic framing paper; establishes reward hacking as a recognized AI safety concern.
42	  - BibTeX key: `amodei2016concrete`
43	
44	- **Open Problems and Fundamental Limitations of RLHF** (Casper et al., 2023, TMLR)
45	  - Key finding: Comprehensive survey. Identifies reward overoptimization as core RLHF failure mode where proxy-aligned policy regresses on true generalization.
46	  - Relevance: Provides survey context; our work adds a neurosymbolic case study to their taxonomy.
47	  - BibTeX key: `casper2023open`
48	
49	- **Consequences of Misaligned AI** (Zhuang & Hadfield-Menell, 2020, NeurIPS)
50	  - Key finding: When agent's reward covers J < L true features, optimizing proxy reliably loses principal utility. Formal Goodhart demonstration from incomplete objectives.
51	  - Relevance: ISR captures one aspect of formalization quality but not all — incomplete proxy, consistent with their framework.
52	  - BibTeX key: `zhuang2020consequences`
53	
54	- **Reward Tampering Problems and Solutions in RL** (Everitt, Hutter, Kumar & Krakovna, 2021, Synthese)
55	  - Key finding: Distinguishes reward tampering (agent modifies own reward signal) from reward hacking (exploiting proxy misspecification) via causal influence diagrams.
56	  - Relevance: Helps clarify that our phenomenon is proxy misspecification (hacking), not tampering.
57	  - BibTeX key: `everitt2021reward`
58	
59	---
60	
61	## Category 2: Verification-Based Reward Signals
62	
63	### Formal Verification as Reward
64	
65	- **RLSF: Reinforcement Learning via Symbolic Feedback** (Jha et al., 2024, arXiv)
66	  - Key finding: Symbolic reasoning tools (solvers, provers) provide fine-grained, token-level feedback via poly-sized certificates. Outperforms traditional approaches on program synthesis (+31.4%), chemistry (+5.5-33.7%), and Game of 24 (+25%). Smaller RLSF models outperform GPT-4.
67	  - Relevance: Most directly relevant — uses solver/prover certificates as reward signal, same paradigm as our ISR. They show it works; we show when it breaks (Goodhart).
68	  - BibTeX key: `jha2024rlsf`
69	
70	- **FoVer: Generalizable Process Reward Models via Formally Verified Training Data** (Kamoi et al., 2025, Findings of ACL 2026)
71	  - Key finding: Uses Z3 and Isabelle to synthesize PRM training data by annotating step-level error labels. Eliminates human annotation. Competitive results on ProcessBench and 12 reasoning benchmarks.
72	  - Relevance: Uses formal verification tools (including Z3, same family as our solver) to generate training signal. Shows verification-based rewards work — we extend by showing dose-response dynamics.
73	  - BibTeX key: `kamoi2025fover`
74	
75	- **SatLM: Satisfiability-Aided Language Models Using Declarative Prompting** (Ye et al., 2023, NeurIPS)
76	  - Key finding: LLM generates declarative specifications; automated theorem prover derives final answer. Outperforms imperative approaches by 23% on GSM hard subset.
77	  - Relevance: Establishes solver-as-verifier paradigm at inference time. Our work uses it at training time as reward.
78	  - BibTeX key: `ye2023satlm`
79	
80	### Proof Assistants as Reward (Math Reasoning)
81	
82	- **DeepSeek-Prover-V1.5: Harnessing Proof Assistant Feedback for RL and MCTS** (DeepSeek AI, 2024, ICLR 2025)
83	  - Key finding: Uses GRPO with Lean 4 verification as binary reward. Achieves 63.5% on miniF2F.
84	  - Relevance: Same algorithm (GRPO) + formal verification reward, but binary (pass/fail). Our ISR is graded, which creates more Goodhart surface.
85	  - BibTeX key: `deepseekprover2024v15`
86	
87	- **AlphaProof** (Google DeepMind, 2024, Nature 2025)
88	  - Key finding: AlphaZero-inspired RL with Lean proof verification. Silver medal at IMO 2024. Binary correctness guarantee via formal verification.
89	  - Relevance: Demonstrates verification-reward RL at scale. Binary reward avoids the Goodhart problem we identify with graded metrics.
90	  - BibTeX key: `alphaproof2024`
91	
92	- **Let's Verify Step by Step** (Lightman et al., 2023, ICLR 2024)
93	  - Key finding: Process supervision (step-level rewards) significantly outperforms outcome supervision on MATH. Released PRM800K.
94	  - Relevance: Establishes that finer-grained verification signals improve training — our ISR is a form of process-level verification reward.
95	  - BibTeX key: `lightman2024lets`
96	
97	- **Math-Shepherd: Verify and Reinforce LLMs Step-by-step without Human Annotations** (Wang, Li et al., 2023, ACL 2024)
98	  - Key finding: Automatically constructs process supervision data. Used as both verifier and step-by-step PPO reward model. Improved Mistral-7B on GSM8K (77.9→84.1%) and MATH (28.6→33.0%).
99	  - Relevance: Automated verification reward without human labels, similar to our automated ISR computation.
100	  - BibTeX key: `wang2024mathshepherd`
101	
102	### Code Execution as Reward
103	
104	- **CodeRL: Mastering Code Generation through Pretrained Models and Deep RL** (Le et al., 2022, NeurIPS)
105	  - Key finding: Actor-critic framework with unit test execution as reward signal. Token-level value estimation guides fine-tuning.
106	  - Relevance: Execution-based verification reward for code; our ISR is solver-based verification for logical formalization.
107	  - BibTeX key: `le2022coderl`
108	
109	- **RLEF: Grounding Code LLMs in Execution Feedback with Reinforcement Learning** (Gehring et al., 2024, ICML 2025)
110	  - Key finding: End-to-end RL with code execution feedback as reward. Large gains on competitive programming with 8B and 70B models.
111	  - Relevance: Shows verification-based RL scales; raises question of whether Goodhart effects emerge at larger scale.
112	  - BibTeX key: `gehring2024rlef`
113	
114	### GRPO with Verifiable Rewards
115	
116	- **DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability via Reinforcement Learning** (DeepSeek AI, 2025, Nature 2026)
117	  - Key finding: Pure RLVR using GRPO produces emergent reasoning without human-labeled traces. Binary rewards from string matching (math) and unit tests (code).
118	  - Relevance: Demonstrates GRPO + verifiable reward at scale. Binary reward sidesteps the graded-metric Goodhart risk we identify.
119	  - BibTeX key: `deepseekr1_2025`
120	
121	- **DeepSeekMath: Pushing the Limits of Mathematical Reasoning** (Shao et al., 2024, arXiv)
122	  - Key finding: Introduced GRPO — estimates advantages via Monte Carlo rollouts within groups, eliminating the critic model.
123	  - Relevance: The algorithm we use. Understanding GRPO mechanics is key to explaining why ISR reward interacts with it as it does.
124	  - BibTeX key: `shao2024deepseekmath`
125	
126	---
127	
128	## Category 3: Auxiliary Reward Dose-Response
129	
130	### KL/Beta Scaling Laws
131	
132	- **Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization in Direct Alignment Algorithms** (Rafailov, Chittepu, Park et al., 2024, NeurIPS)
133	  - Key finding: Extends Gao et al. to DPO/IPO/SLiC. Tests seven beta values across 1B-6.9B models. DAAs still overoptimize despite no explicit proxy RM. Smaller models overoptimize sooner.
134	  - Relevance: Direct evidence that beta-controlled dose-response is a general phenomenon, not specific to PPO-style RLHF. Validates studying β as a "dose" parameter.
135	  - BibTeX key: `rafailov2024scaling`
136	
137	- **Correcting the Mythos of KL-Regularization: Chi-Squared Preference Optimization** (Huang et al., 2025, ICLR Spotlight)
138	  - Key finding: KL-regularization is theoretically inadequate for preventing overoptimization. Chi-squared divergence provably alleviates it.
139	  - Relevance: Suggests that even with KL penalty in GRPO, overoptimization (our high-β collapse) is theoretically expected. Alternative divergence measures could help.
140	  - BibTeX key: `huang2025correcting`
141	
142	- **Provably Mitigating Overoptimization in RLHF** (Liu et al., 2024, NeurIPS)
143	  - Key finding: Distributional shift causes overoptimization. SFT loss acts as pessimistic regularizer against spuriously high proxy rewards.
144	  - Relevance: Our high-β ISR collapse may involve distributional shift — policy moves to regions where ISR is high but quality is low.
145	  - BibTeX key: `liu2024provably`
146	
147	### Multi-Objective Reward Weighting
148	
149	- **Multi-Objective Direct Preference Optimization (MODPO)** (Zhou, Li et al., 2024, Findings of ACL)
150	  - Key finding: Extends DPO to multiple alignment objectives. Produces Pareto fronts showing how objective weight ratios control safety-helpfulness trade-off.
151	  - Relevance: Our exec+ISR is a multi-objective problem. MODPO's Pareto analysis framework could formalize our β sweep results.
152	  - BibTeX key: `zhou2024modpo`
153	
154	- **ArmoRM: Interpretable Preferences via Multi-Objective Reward Modeling and MoE** (Wang, Xiong et al., 2024, Findings of EMNLP)
155	  - Key finding: MoE gating auto-selects reward objective weights per context. Fixed uniform weights are suboptimal.
156	  - Relevance: Suggests per-instance β (rather than fixed β) could avoid Goodhart effects.
157	  - BibTeX key: `wang2024armorm`
158	
159	- **Reward Model Ensembles Help Mitigate Overoptimization** (Coste et al., 2023, NeurIPS Workshop)
160	  - Key finding: Worst-case optimization across RM ensembles practically eliminates overoptimization for BoN and reduces it for PPO.
161	  - Relevance: Ensemble approach as mitigation; could apply to our ISR (multiple solver metrics instead of one).
162	  - BibTeX key: `coste2023reward`
163	
164	### Adaptive Auxiliary Reward Weighting
165	
166	- **Learning to Utilize Shaping Rewards (BiPaRS)** (Hu et al., 2020, NeurIPS)
167	  - Key finding: Bi-level optimization learns parameterized shaping reward weights. Can even transform harmful shaping rewards into beneficial ones by learning negative weights.
168	  - Relevance: Directly addresses our problem — when auxiliary reward (ISR) weight is wrong, automated weight learning could find optimal β.
169	  - BibTeX key: `hu2020bipars`
170	
171	- **Reward Training Wheels: Adaptive Auxiliary Rewards for Robotics RL** (Wang, Xu et al., 2025, IROS)
172	  - Key finding: Teacher dynamically adjusts auxiliary reward weights based on student's evolving capabilities. Optimal auxiliary weight is stage-dependent.
173	  - Relevance: Suggests β should decrease during training as the policy improves — matches intuition that ISR is useful early but harmful when over-optimized.
174	  - BibTeX key: `wang2025reward`
175	
176	- **Automatic Successive RL with Multiple Auxiliary Rewards (ASR)** (Fu, Zhan et al., 2019, IJCAI)
177	  - Key finding: Fixed linear scalarization is suboptimal; ASR dynamically selects which auxiliary reward to emphasize at each training stage.
178	  - Relevance: Supports the idea that a fixed β throughout training is inherently limited.
179	  - BibTeX key: `fu2019automatic`
180	
181	- **Adaptive Reward Scaling for Multi-Task RL (ARS)** (Cho, Park, Kim & Sung, 2025, ICML)
182	  - Key finding: History-based reward scaling ensures balanced reward distributions across tasks. Unbalanced magnitudes cause catastrophic interference.
183	  - Relevance: Our ISR at high β may dominate the exec reward signal, causing the catastrophic PR collapse we observe.
184	  - BibTeX key: `cho2025ars`
185	
186	- **UNREAL: RL with Unsupervised Auxiliary Tasks** (Jaderberg et al., 2017, ICLR)
187	  - Key finding: Foundational auxiliary-task paper. Auxiliary task weights (λ) are domain-dependent; different ranges needed for different environments.
188	  - Relevance: Classic reference establishing that auxiliary reward weight tuning is critical and domain-specific.
189	  - BibTeX key: `jaderberg2017unreal`
190	
191	### GRPO-Specific
192	
193	- **DAPO: An Open-Source LLM Reinforcement Learning System at Scale** (Yu et al., ByteDance, 2025, arXiv)
194	  - Key finding: Four techniques for stable multi-component reward: Clip-Higher, Dynamic Sampling, token-level policy gradient, Overlong Reward Shaping with soft punishment.
195	  - Relevance: GRPO variant with multiple reward components; their techniques address stability issues relevant to our multi-reward setup.
196	  - BibTeX key: `yu2025dapo`
197	
198	---
199	
200	## Positioning Summary
201	
202	### Novelty (what we contribute that prior work doesn't cover)
203	
204	1. **First Goodhart characterization in neurosymbolic verification rewards**: Prior work studies reward hacking in language preference RMs (Gao et al.), game environments (Pan et al.), or code execution (CodeRL). No one has studied Goodhart effects when a logical solver's output is used as RL reward signal.
205	
206	2. **Dose-response curve for verification-based auxiliary reward**: We provide the first empirical β sweep showing inverted-U behavior specifically for a solver-based metric (ISR). Prior dose-response studies are in RLHF preference settings (Rafailov et al.) or robotics (Wang et al.), not formal verification.
207	
208	3. **Qualitative phase transition**: Our β=0.1→0.3 transition shows a sharp qualitative shift (PR 81%→18%), not a smooth degradation. This connects to Pan et al.'s phase transitions but in a neurosymbolic context.
209	
210	4. **Graded vs. binary verification rewards**: We implicitly show that graded metrics (ISR) are more Goodhart-susceptible than binary verification (pass/fail used by DeepSeek-Prover, AlphaProof, DeepSeek-R1). This distinction hasn't been articulated in prior literature.
211	
212	### Citable Support (what prior work validates)
213	
214	- **Inverted-U is a known pattern**: Gao et al. 2023, Rafailov et al. 2024 establish this for RLHF; we confirm it extends to solver-based rewards.
215	- **Proxy hacking is theoretically inevitable**: Skalse et al. 2022 prove no non-trivial unhackable proxy exists; our ISR hacking is a predicted consequence.
216	- **Goodhart taxonomy applies**: Manheim & Garrabrant 2019 — our case is extremal/causal Goodhart.
217	- **Verification rewards work at low dose**: Lightman et al. 2024, RLSF 2024, Math-Shepherd 2024 show verification signals improve training; consistent with our β=0.1 result.
218	- **Composite rewards need careful balancing**: Moskovitz et al. 2024 show correlation between reward components affects overoptimization onset.
219	
220	### Anticipated Reviewer Questions
221	
222	1. **"Why not use binary ISR instead of graded?"** — Binary (solved/unsolved) would likely avoid Goodhart but lose the richer training signal. This is an explicit trade-off we should discuss citing DeepSeek-Prover/AlphaProof (binary works) vs. Lightman/Math-Shepherd (graded is richer).
223	
224	2. **"How does this relate to Gao et al. scaling laws?"** — Our β sweep is analogous to their KL sweep. We should plot our results in their framework (gold reward vs. proxy optimization intensity).
225	
226	3. **"Why not use adaptive β?"** — BiPaRS, ASR, ARS show adaptive weighting outperforms fixed. We should acknowledge this as future work and cite these papers.
227	
228	4. **"Is this just reward shaping gone wrong?"** — Partially, but it's specifically Goodhart (measure→target→ceases to be good measure), not generic reward shaping failure. Manheim & Garrabrant's taxonomy helps distinguish.
229	
230	5. **"What's the Goodhart mechanism — regressional, extremal, causal, or adversarial?"** — Likely extremal (policy finds OOD region where ISR↑ but quality↓) with possible causal component (ISR correlates with quality in training distribution but the correlation breaks under optimization pressure).

# Goodhart's Law in RL — Literature Survey

## Category 1: Reward Overoptimization in RLHF

### Core Papers

- **Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization** (Gao, Schulman & Hilton, 2023, ICML)
  - Key finding: Gold reward initially increases then decreases as optimization against proxy RM intensifies — direct empirical Goodhart demonstration. The overoptimization relationship follows different functional forms for RL vs. best-of-n, coefficients scale smoothly with RM parameter count. KL penalties increase achievable proxy reward at a given KL but do not improve the gold-reward frontier.
  - Relevance: Foundational paper. Our ISR dose-response (β=0.1 helps, β=0.3 hurts) is a precise instance of their inverted-U curve, but in a neurosymbolic verification setting rather than language preference.
  - BibTeX key: `gao2023scaling`

- **Defining and Characterizing Reward Hacking** (Skalse, Howe, Krasheninnikov & Krueger, 2022, NeurIPS)
  - Key finding: First formal definition of reward hacking. Proves that for stochastic policies, non-trivial unhackable proxy-true reward pairs do not exist (unless one is constant). Establishes reward hacking as a near-universal theoretical concern.
  - Relevance: Provides the theoretical impossibility result that frames why our ISR hacking is expected, not anomalous.
  - BibTeX key: `skalse2022defining`

- **Categorizing Variants of Goodhart's Law** (Manheim & Garrabrant, 2019, arXiv)
  - Key finding: Four-part taxonomy: (1) Regressional — extreme proxy values overestimate true goal; (2) Extremal — proxy-goal relationship breaks in OOD regions; (3) Causal — non-causal correlations fail under intervention; (4) Adversarial — optimization creates gaming incentives.
  - Relevance: Our high-β ISR collapse is best classified as extremal Goodhart (policy moves to OOD region where ISR↑ but PR↓). Provides vocabulary for discussion section.
  - BibTeX key: `manheim2019categorizing`

- **The Effects of Reward Misspecification: Mapping and Mitigating Misaligned Models** (Pan, Bhatia & Steinhardt, 2022, ICLR)
  - Key finding: Across 9 environments, more capable agents exploit misspecifications more. Observes phase transitions — capability thresholds where true reward sharply drops. Proposes anomaly detection as mitigation.
  - Relevance: Their "phase transition" pattern matches our β=0.1→0.3 discontinuity. More capable optimization = worse outcome under misspecification.
  - BibTeX key: `pan2022effects`

- **Confronting Reward Model Overoptimization with Constrained RLHF** (Moskovitz, Singh, Strouse et al., 2024, ICLR Spotlight)
  - Key finding: First study of overoptimization in composite reward models. Correlation between component RMs affects overoptimization onset. Proposes constrained RL to prevent exceeding each component's "threshold of usefulness."
  - Relevance: Directly applicable — our setup combines exec reward + ISR reward. Their "threshold of usefulness" concept maps to our optimal β.
  - BibTeX key: `moskovitz2024confronting`

- **Catastrophic Goodhart: Regularizing RLHF with KL Divergence Does Not Mitigate Heavy-Tailed Reward Misspecification** (Kwa, Thomas & Garriga-Alonso, 2024, NeurIPS)
  - Key finding: If reward model error is heavy-tailed, policies can achieve arbitrarily high proxy reward with no true utility gain. KL regularization provably fails under heavy-tailed misspecification.
  - Relevance: Raises the question of whether our ISR error distribution is heavy-tailed — if so, explains why KL penalty alone cannot prevent collapse at high β.
  - BibTeX key: `kwa2024catastrophic`

### Survey & Background

- **Concrete Problems in AI Safety** (Amodei, Olah, Steinhardt et al., 2016, arXiv)
  - Key finding: Identifies reward hacking as one of five practical AI safety problems. Discusses exploitation through environmental complexity and hard-to-formalize concepts.
  - Relevance: Classic framing paper; establishes reward hacking as a recognized AI safety concern.
  - BibTeX key: `amodei2016concrete`

- **Open Problems and Fundamental Limitations of RLHF** (Casper et al., 2023, TMLR)
  - Key finding: Comprehensive survey. Identifies reward overoptimization as core RLHF failure mode where proxy-aligned policy regresses on true generalization.
  - Relevance: Provides survey context; our work adds a neurosymbolic case study to their taxonomy.
  - BibTeX key: `casper2023open`

- **Consequences of Misaligned AI** (Zhuang & Hadfield-Menell, 2020, NeurIPS)
  - Key finding: When agent's reward covers J < L true features, optimizing proxy reliably loses principal utility. Formal Goodhart demonstration from incomplete objectives.
  - Relevance: ISR captures one aspect of formalization quality but not all — incomplete proxy, consistent with their framework.
  - BibTeX key: `zhuang2020consequences`

- **Reward Tampering Problems and Solutions in RL** (Everitt, Hutter, Kumar & Krakovna, 2021, Synthese)
  - Key finding: Distinguishes reward tampering (agent modifies own reward signal) from reward hacking (exploiting proxy misspecification) via causal influence diagrams.
  - Relevance: Helps clarify that our phenomenon is proxy misspecification (hacking), not tampering.
  - BibTeX key: `everitt2021reward`

---

## Category 2: Verification-Based Reward Signals

### Formal Verification as Reward

- **RLSF: Reinforcement Learning via Symbolic Feedback** (Jha et al., 2024, arXiv)
  - Key finding: Symbolic reasoning tools (solvers, provers) provide fine-grained, token-level feedback via poly-sized certificates. Outperforms traditional approaches on program synthesis (+31.4%), chemistry (+5.5-33.7%), and Game of 24 (+25%). Smaller RLSF models outperform GPT-4.
  - Relevance: Most directly relevant — uses solver/prover certificates as reward signal, same paradigm as our ISR. They show it works; we show when it breaks (Goodhart).
  - BibTeX key: `jha2024rlsf`

- **FoVer: Generalizable Process Reward Models via Formally Verified Training Data** (Kamoi et al., 2025, Findings of ACL 2026)
  - Key finding: Uses Z3 and Isabelle to synthesize PRM training data by annotating step-level error labels. Eliminates human annotation. Competitive results on ProcessBench and 12 reasoning benchmarks.
  - Relevance: Uses formal verification tools (including Z3, same family as our solver) to generate training signal. Shows verification-based rewards work — we extend by showing dose-response dynamics.
  - BibTeX key: `kamoi2025fover`

- **SatLM: Satisfiability-Aided Language Models Using Declarative Prompting** (Ye et al., 2023, NeurIPS)
  - Key finding: LLM generates declarative specifications; automated theorem prover derives final answer. Outperforms imperative approaches by 23% on GSM hard subset.
  - Relevance: Establishes solver-as-verifier paradigm at inference time. Our work uses it at training time as reward.
  - BibTeX key: `ye2023satlm`

### Proof Assistants as Reward (Math Reasoning)

- **DeepSeek-Prover-V1.5: Harnessing Proof Assistant Feedback for RL and MCTS** (DeepSeek AI, 2024, ICLR 2025)
  - Key finding: Uses GRPO with Lean 4 verification as binary reward. Achieves 63.5% on miniF2F.
  - Relevance: Same algorithm (GRPO) + formal verification reward, but binary (pass/fail). Our ISR is graded, which creates more Goodhart surface.
  - BibTeX key: `deepseekprover2024v15`

- **AlphaProof** (Google DeepMind, 2024, Nature 2025)
  - Key finding: AlphaZero-inspired RL with Lean proof verification. Silver medal at IMO 2024. Binary correctness guarantee via formal verification.
  - Relevance: Demonstrates verification-reward RL at scale. Binary reward avoids the Goodhart problem we identify with graded metrics.
  - BibTeX key: `alphaproof2024`

- **Let's Verify Step by Step** (Lightman et al., 2023, ICLR 2024)
  - Key finding: Process supervision (step-level rewards) significantly outperforms outcome supervision on MATH. Released PRM800K.
  - Relevance: Establishes that finer-grained verification signals improve training — our ISR is a form of process-level verification reward.
  - BibTeX key: `lightman2024lets`

- **Math-Shepherd: Verify and Reinforce LLMs Step-by-step without Human Annotations** (Wang, Li et al., 2023, ACL 2024)
  - Key finding: Automatically constructs process supervision data. Used as both verifier and step-by-step PPO reward model. Improved Mistral-7B on GSM8K (77.9→84.1%) and MATH (28.6→33.0%).
  - Relevance: Automated verification reward without human labels, similar to our automated ISR computation.
  - BibTeX key: `wang2024mathshepherd`

### Code Execution as Reward

- **CodeRL: Mastering Code Generation through Pretrained Models and Deep RL** (Le et al., 2022, NeurIPS)
  - Key finding: Actor-critic framework with unit test execution as reward signal. Token-level value estimation guides fine-tuning.
  - Relevance: Execution-based verification reward for code; our ISR is solver-based verification for logical formalization.
  - BibTeX key: `le2022coderl`

- **RLEF: Grounding Code LLMs in Execution Feedback with Reinforcement Learning** (Gehring et al., 2024, ICML 2025)
  - Key finding: End-to-end RL with code execution feedback as reward. Large gains on competitive programming with 8B and 70B models.
  - Relevance: Shows verification-based RL scales; raises question of whether Goodhart effects emerge at larger scale.
  - BibTeX key: `gehring2024rlef`

### GRPO with Verifiable Rewards

- **DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability via Reinforcement Learning** (DeepSeek AI, 2025, Nature 2026)
  - Key finding: Pure RLVR using GRPO produces emergent reasoning without human-labeled traces. Binary rewards from string matching (math) and unit tests (code).
  - Relevance: Demonstrates GRPO + verifiable reward at scale. Binary reward sidesteps the graded-metric Goodhart risk we identify.
  - BibTeX key: `deepseekr1_2025`

- **DeepSeekMath: Pushing the Limits of Mathematical Reasoning** (Shao et al., 2024, arXiv)
  - Key finding: Introduced GRPO — estimates advantages via Monte Carlo rollouts within groups, eliminating the critic model.
  - Relevance: The algorithm we use. Understanding GRPO mechanics is key to explaining why ISR reward interacts with it as it does.
  - BibTeX key: `shao2024deepseekmath`

---

## Category 3: Auxiliary Reward Dose-Response

### KL/Beta Scaling Laws

- **Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization in Direct Alignment Algorithms** (Rafailov, Chittepu, Park et al., 2024, NeurIPS)
  - Key finding: Extends Gao et al. to DPO/IPO/SLiC. Tests seven beta values across 1B-6.9B models. DAAs still overoptimize despite no explicit proxy RM. Smaller models overoptimize sooner.
  - Relevance: Direct evidence that beta-controlled dose-response is a general phenomenon, not specific to PPO-style RLHF. Validates studying β as a "dose" parameter.
  - BibTeX key: `rafailov2024scaling`

- **Correcting the Mythos of KL-Regularization: Chi-Squared Preference Optimization** (Huang et al., 2025, ICLR Spotlight)
  - Key finding: KL-regularization is theoretically inadequate for preventing overoptimization. Chi-squared divergence provably alleviates it.
  - Relevance: Suggests that even with KL penalty in GRPO, overoptimization (our high-β collapse) is theoretically expected. Alternative divergence measures could help.
  - BibTeX key: `huang2025correcting`

- **Provably Mitigating Overoptimization in RLHF** (Liu et al., 2024, NeurIPS)
  - Key finding: Distributional shift causes overoptimization. SFT loss acts as pessimistic regularizer against spuriously high proxy rewards.
  - Relevance: Our high-β ISR collapse may involve distributional shift — policy moves to regions where ISR is high but quality is low.
  - BibTeX key: `liu2024provably`

### Multi-Objective Reward Weighting

- **Multi-Objective Direct Preference Optimization (MODPO)** (Zhou, Li et al., 2024, Findings of ACL)
  - Key finding: Extends DPO to multiple alignment objectives. Produces Pareto fronts showing how objective weight ratios control safety-helpfulness trade-off.
  - Relevance: Our exec+ISR is a multi-objective problem. MODPO's Pareto analysis framework could formalize our β sweep results.
  - BibTeX key: `zhou2024modpo`

- **ArmoRM: Interpretable Preferences via Multi-Objective Reward Modeling and MoE** (Wang, Xiong et al., 2024, Findings of EMNLP)
  - Key finding: MoE gating auto-selects reward objective weights per context. Fixed uniform weights are suboptimal.
  - Relevance: Suggests per-instance β (rather than fixed β) could avoid Goodhart effects.
  - BibTeX key: `wang2024armorm`

- **Reward Model Ensembles Help Mitigate Overoptimization** (Coste et al., 2023, NeurIPS Workshop)
  - Key finding: Worst-case optimization across RM ensembles practically eliminates overoptimization for BoN and reduces it for PPO.
  - Relevance: Ensemble approach as mitigation; could apply to our ISR (multiple solver metrics instead of one).
  - BibTeX key: `coste2023reward`

### Adaptive Auxiliary Reward Weighting

- **Learning to Utilize Shaping Rewards (BiPaRS)** (Hu et al., 2020, NeurIPS)
  - Key finding: Bi-level optimization learns parameterized shaping reward weights. Can even transform harmful shaping rewards into beneficial ones by learning negative weights.
  - Relevance: Directly addresses our problem — when auxiliary reward (ISR) weight is wrong, automated weight learning could find optimal β.
  - BibTeX key: `hu2020bipars`

- **Reward Training Wheels: Adaptive Auxiliary Rewards for Robotics RL** (Wang, Xu et al., 2025, IROS)
  - Key finding: Teacher dynamically adjusts auxiliary reward weights based on student's evolving capabilities. Optimal auxiliary weight is stage-dependent.
  - Relevance: Suggests β should decrease during training as the policy improves — matches intuition that ISR is useful early but harmful when over-optimized.
  - BibTeX key: `wang2025reward`

- **Automatic Successive RL with Multiple Auxiliary Rewards (ASR)** (Fu, Zhan et al., 2019, IJCAI)
  - Key finding: Fixed linear scalarization is suboptimal; ASR dynamically selects which auxiliary reward to emphasize at each training stage.
  - Relevance: Supports the idea that a fixed β throughout training is inherently limited.
  - BibTeX key: `fu2019automatic`

- **Adaptive Reward Scaling for Multi-Task RL (ARS)** (Cho, Park, Kim & Sung, 2025, ICML)
  - Key finding: History-based reward scaling ensures balanced reward distributions across tasks. Unbalanced magnitudes cause catastrophic interference.
  - Relevance: Our ISR at high β may dominate the exec reward signal, causing the catastrophic PR collapse we observe.
  - BibTeX key: `cho2025ars`

- **UNREAL: RL with Unsupervised Auxiliary Tasks** (Jaderberg et al., 2017, ICLR)
  - Key finding: Foundational auxiliary-task paper. Auxiliary task weights (λ) are domain-dependent; different ranges needed for different environments.
  - Relevance: Classic reference establishing that auxiliary reward weight tuning is critical and domain-specific.
  - BibTeX key: `jaderberg2017unreal`

### GRPO-Specific

- **DAPO: An Open-Source LLM Reinforcement Learning System at Scale** (Yu et al., ByteDance, 2025, arXiv)
  - Key finding: Four techniques for stable multi-component reward: Clip-Higher, Dynamic Sampling, token-level policy gradient, Overlong Reward Shaping with soft punishment.
  - Relevance: GRPO variant with multiple reward components; their techniques address stability issues relevant to our multi-reward setup.
  - BibTeX key: `yu2025dapo`

---

## Positioning Summary

### Novelty (what we contribute that prior work doesn't cover)

1. **First Goodhart characterization in neurosymbolic verification rewards**: Prior work studies reward hacking in language preference RMs (Gao et al.), game environments (Pan et al.), or code execution (CodeRL). No one has studied Goodhart effects when a logical solver's output is used as RL reward signal.

2. **Dose-response curve for verification-based auxiliary reward**: We provide the first empirical β sweep showing inverted-U behavior specifically for a solver-based metric (ISR). Prior dose-response studies are in RLHF preference settings (Rafailov et al.) or robotics (Wang et al.), not formal verification.

3. **Qualitative phase transition**: Our β=0.1→0.3 transition shows a sharp qualitative shift (PR 81%→18%), not a smooth degradation. This connects to Pan et al.'s phase transitions but in a neurosymbolic context.

4. **Graded vs. binary verification rewards**: We implicitly show that graded metrics (ISR) are more Goodhart-susceptible than binary verification (pass/fail used by DeepSeek-Prover, AlphaProof, DeepSeek-R1). This distinction hasn't been articulated in prior literature.

### Citable Support (what prior work validates)

- **Inverted-U is a known pattern**: Gao et al. 2023, Rafailov et al. 2024 establish this for RLHF; we confirm it extends to solver-based rewards.
- **Proxy hacking is theoretically inevitable**: Skalse et al. 2022 prove no non-trivial unhackable proxy exists; our ISR hacking is a predicted consequence.
- **Goodhart taxonomy applies**: Manheim & Garrabrant 2019 — our case is extremal/causal Goodhart.
- **Verification rewards work at low dose**: Lightman et al. 2024, RLSF 2024, Math-Shepherd 2024 show verification signals improve training; consistent with our β=0.1 result.
- **Composite rewards need careful balancing**: Moskovitz et al. 2024 show correlation between reward components affects overoptimization onset.

### Anticipated Reviewer Questions

1. **"Why not use binary ISR instead of graded?"** — Binary (solved/unsolved) would likely avoid Goodhart but lose the richer training signal. This is an explicit trade-off we should discuss citing DeepSeek-Prover/AlphaProof (binary works) vs. Lightman/Math-Shepherd (graded is richer).

2. **"How does this relate to Gao et al. scaling laws?"** — Our β sweep is analogous to their KL sweep. We should plot our results in their framework (gold reward vs. proxy optimization intensity).

3. **"Why not use adaptive β?"** — BiPaRS, ASR, ARS show adaptive weighting outperforms fixed. We should acknowledge this as future work and cite these papers.

4. **"Is this just reward shaping gone wrong?"** — Partially, but it's specifically Goodhart (measure→target→ceases to be good measure), not generic reward shaping failure. Manheim & Garrabrant's taxonomy helps distinguish.

5. **"What's the Goodhart mechanism — regressional, extremal, causal, or adversarial?"** — Likely extremal (policy finds OOD region where ISR↑ but quality↓) with possible causal component (ISR correlates with quality in training distribution but the correlation breaks under optimization pressure).

Now I can see all the issues. Let me fix them:

1. **FoVer venue**: Line 70 in literature_goodhart.md already has "Findings of ACL 2026" — looks correct. But in literature_map.yaml, the `fover` entry (not `fover-prm`) says "TACL 13:1340-1359". The `fover-prm` entry says "arXiv 2502.01345". Director said FoVer (Kamoi et al.) has been accepted to ACL 2026 Findings.

Let me check: there are TWO FoVer entries:

### KL/Beta Scaling Laws

- **Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization in Direct Alignment Algorithms** (Rafailov, Chittepu, Park et al., 2024, NeurIPS)
  - Key finding: Extends Gao et al. to DPO/IPO/SLiC. Tests seven beta values across 1B-6.9B models. DAAs still overoptimize despite no explicit proxy RM. Smaller models overoptimize sooner.
  - Relevance: Direct evidence that beta-controlled dose-response is a general phenomenon, not specific to PPO-style RLHF. Validates studying β as a "dose" parameter.
  - BibTeX key: `rafailov2024scaling`

- **Correcting the Mythos of KL-Regularization: Chi-Squared Preference Optimization** (Huang et al., 2025, ICLR 2025 Poster)
  - Key finding: KL-regularization is theoretically inadequate for preventing overoptimization. Chi-squared divergence provably alleviates it.
  - Relevance: Suggests that even with KL penalty in GRPO, overoptimization (our high-β collapse) is theoretically expected. Alternative divergence measures could help.
  - BibTeX key: `huang2025correcting`

- **Provably Mitigating Overoptimization in RLHF** (Liu et al., 2024, NeurIPS)
  - Key finding: Distributional shift causes overoptimization. SFT loss acts as pessimistic regularizer against spuriously high proxy rewards.
  - Relevance: Our high-β ISR collapse may involve distributional shift — policy moves to regions where ISR is high but quality is low.

1. **首个在 neurosymbolic verification reward 上刻画 Goodhart 效应**：已有工作研究 RLHF preference RM (Gao et al. 2023)、game 环境 (Pan et al. 2022)、code execution (CodeRL) 的 reward hacking，无人研究 logical solver output 作为 RL reward 时的 Goodhart
2. **Verification-based auxiliary reward 的剂量响应曲线**：首个 β sweep 展示 solver-based metric (ISR) 的倒 U 型行为。已有 dose-response 研究在 RLHF preference (Rafailov et al. 2024) 或 robotics (Wang et al. 2025)，不在 formal verification
3. **定性 phase transition**：β=0.1→0.3 从 PR 81%→18% 的急剧跳变，连接 Pan et al. 的 phase transition 但在 neurosymbolic 上下文
4. **Graded vs binary verification reward 的 Goodhart 易感性差异**：graded ISR 比 binary pass/fail (DeepSeek-Prover/AlphaProof/DeepSeek-R1) 更易被 hack——此区分在已有文献中尚无人明确指出

### Goodhart 分类
- 我们的 high-β ISR collapse = **extremal Goodhart** (Manheim & Garrabrant 2019)：policy 移到 ISR↑ 但 PR↓ 的 OOD 区域
- 可能有 **causal Goodhart** 成分：ISR 和 quality 的相关性在优化压力下断裂

---

## Positioning Summary

### Novelty (what we contribute that prior work doesn't cover)

1. **First Goodhart characterization in neurosymbolic verification rewards**: Prior work studies reward hacking in language preference RMs (Gao et al.), game environments (Pan et al.), or code execution (CodeRL). No one has studied Goodhart effects when a logical solver's output is used as RL reward signal.

2. **Dose-response curve for verification-based auxiliary reward**: We provide the first empirical β sweep showing inverted-U behavior specifically for a solver-based metric (ISR). Prior dose-response studies are in RLHF preference settings (Rafailov et al.) or robotics (Wang et al.), not formal verification.

3. **Dose-dependent qualitative shift**: Our β=0.1→0.3 transition shows a qualitative shift (PR 81%→18%), not a smooth degradation. This connects to Pan et al.'s dose-dependent dynamics but in a neurosymbolic context. (Note: only 2 β values tested; finer-grained β sweep needed to characterize the transition shape.)

### Citable Support (what prior work validates)

- **Inverted-U is a known pattern**: Gao et al. 2023, Rafailov et al. 2024 establish this for RLHF; we confirm it extends to solver-based rewards.
- **Proxy hacking is theoretically inevitable**: Skalse et al. 2022 prove no non-trivial unhackable proxy exists; our ISR hacking is a predicted consequence.
- **Goodhart taxonomy applies**: Manheim & Garrabrant 2019 — our case is extremal/causal Goodhart.
- **Verification rewards work at low dose**: Lightman et al. 2024, RLSF 2024, Math-Shepherd 2024 show verification signals improve training; consistent with our β=0.1 result.
- **Composite rewards need careful balancing**: Moskovitz et al. 2024 show correlation between reward components affects overoptimization onset.

### Anticipated Reviewer Questions

1. **"Why not use binary ISR instead of graded?"** — Binary (solved/unsolved) would likely avoid Goodhart but lose the richer training signal. This is an explicit trade-off we should discuss citing DeepSeek-Prover/AlphaProof (binary works) vs. Lightman/Math-Shepherd (graded is richer).

2. **"How does this relate to Gao et al. scaling laws?"** — Our β sweep is analogous to their KL sweep. We should plot our results in their framework (gold reward vs. proxy optimization intensity).

3. **"Why not use adaptive β?"** — BiPaRS, ASR, ARS show adaptive weighting outperforms fixed. We should acknowledge this as future work and cite these papers.

4. **"Is this just reward shaping gone wrong?"** — Partially, but it's specifically Goodhart (measure→target→ceases to be good measure), not generic reward shaping failure. Manheim & Garrabrant's taxonomy helps distinguish.

5. **"What's the Goodhart mechanism — regressional, extremal, causal, or adversarial?"** — Likely extremal (policy finds OOD region where ISR↑ but quality↓) with possible causal component (ISR correlates with quality in training distribution but the correlation breaks under optimization pressure).

---

## Discussion / Future Work
